newsitem.title: UK: Trelleborg to boost Ronnskar copper output by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Trelleborg to boost Ronnskar copper output by 2000.

text.p: Boliden AB, the mining arm of Swedish group Trelleborg AB, aims to boost refined copper production at its Ronnskar plant to 210,000 tonnes a year by 2000 against the 130,000 tonnes expected in 1996.

Anders Bulow, president of Boliden, told an Association of Mining Analysts presentation on Monday that the group also planned to increase refined zinc production to 148,000 tonnes by 2000 from 130,000 this year.
"We are going to see a substantial surplus of copper concentrates over the next few years, and that will need a home giving us very good terms for the Ronnskar operation," he said.
Although the group was bearish about copper prices in the medium term, a growing concentrates surplus would push up refining and treatment charges, benefiting the group, he explained.
"We are assured a relatively low copper price for two years ahead," he said.
The outlook for zinc, the most important single product for the group, was more positive.
"We are going to see a positive price trend for zinc in the near term," Bulow said. "What seems to be overhanging the market is this Asturiana position," he added.
Bulow was referring to a long position on the London Metal Exchange (LME) which Spanish producer Asturiana de Zinc is understood to have taken on in 1992, when prices were high.
Asturiana reportedly transferred the position to trading firm Glencore, which will manage it from now on.
Bulow was bearish for lead, Boliden's other main base metal product. "We are not building plans on such a high level of lead price as we have enjoyed this year," he said.
Bulow said the company's Swedish lead mine would be closed when prices fell below the "critical level", although he would not specify what the level was.
He added that the company had in place a hedge programme that would avert "nasty surprises" in the lead market for the time being.
Boliden aimed to boost its production of recycled lead each year to 50,000 tonnes by the start of the next century against 40,600 tonnes in 1996, according to Bulow.
The recycling plant in the south of Sweden got its battery scrap feed domestically, from other Scandinavian countries and from some eastern European destinations.
"We also see Russia as a potential contributor, especially since they signed the Basle Convention," Bulow said.

Bulow said he expected to see the development of increasingly big ore bodies over the coming years as part of a drive towards greater cost efficiency. He also expected mining companies to become fewer and larger.
"Our ambition is to become one of those," he said.
